unit.title: Provide temporary epilation and bleaching treatments

summary: This unit teaches you to remove unwanted hair temporarily and to lighten it safely. You will learn how hair grows, how to consult and check for contraindications, how to set up a wax heater and test the temperature, and how to give warm (strip) wax, hot (hard) wax and sugaring treatments. You will also learn to give a hair bleaching treatment, deal with contra-actions and burns, give aftercare advice and keep records.

blocks.p: This unit covers temporary hair removal and hair lightening, from the first question you ask a client to the last wipe of the wax heater. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. Waxing and bleaching are popular services, and clients return for them every few weeks, so a careful, hygienic therapist builds a loyal clientele.

These services can also hurt a client. Hot wax can burn, wax can tear thin skin, a dirty spatula can spread infection, and bleach can burn or cause an allergy. That is why this unit is about **checking, testing, temperature control and hygiene** as much as technique.

Use for the underarm, bikini line, lip and brows
Know how sugaring paste works
Give bleaching treatments

Deal with contra-actions and first aid

Advise and record

Consult and check

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks. In one you give a half-leg wax with warm (strip) wax. In the other you give a forearm bleach (after a skin test) and a hot wax treatment on a small area. The assessor watches your checks, temperature testing, hygiene, method, aftercare and records, not only the finished skin.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the work area (the legs, the arm), never a client's face or private areas, and only with her agreement.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Term
What it means
Examples
rows: Epilation
Removing hair **from the root**. The result lasts longer, usually 4 to 6 weeks.
Waxing, sugaring, threading, tweezing
Depilation
Removing hair **at the surface** of the skin. Hair returns within days.
Shaving, depilatory (hair-removing) creams, trimming
Temporary
Hair grows back, so the treatment must be repeated.
All of the above
Permanent hair reduction
Treatments that damage the follicle, such as electrolysis or laser. Not part of this unit.
Electrolysis, laser
Bleaching
Lightening the colour of dark hair so that it shows less. It does **not** remove the hair, and it does not lighten the skin.
Forearm or upper-lip hair bleach

head: Type
What it is like
Where
rows: Lanugo
Very fine, soft hair that covers an unborn baby.
Before birth
Vellus
Fine, soft, short, light hair that covers most of the body.
Face, arms, body
Terminal
Thick, coarse, longer, darker hair.
Scalp, brows, lashes; under the arms and pubic area; legs and, in men, face and chest

blocks.p: Hormones at puberty turn vellus hair into terminal hair in some areas. Changes in hormones, some medicines and some medical conditions can also cause extra hair to grow; if a client has a sudden increase, advise her to see a doctor.

blocks.h: The follicle and the hair growth cycle

blocks.p: Each hair grows from a **follicle**, a small pocket in the skin. At the base of the follicle, the **papilla** feeds the hair with blood. Each follicle has a sebaceous gland that oils the hair and a tiny muscle that makes the hair stand up.

head: Stage
What happens
Waxing and the cycle
rows: Anagen (growing)
The hair is attached to its blood supply at the base of the follicle and grows actively.
Waxing works best when most hairs are in anagen, because they are firmly rooted and the whole root comes out.
Catagen (changing)
A short stage: the hair stops growing and comes away from its blood supply.
A short stage, so it matters little for planning; the hair is about to rest.
Telogen (resting)
The hair is loose in the follicle until it falls out or a new hair pushes it out.
Loose hairs may come out easily; others remain on their way up.

ul: Every hair is at a different stage, so after a wax some hairs reappear within days (hairs that were not yet through the skin), while others take weeks.
Waxing every **4 to 6 weeks** is usual. With regular treatment more hairs fall into step and the skin looks smoother for longer.
Waxing does **not** make hair grow back thicker or darker. Shaving cuts the hair at its widest part, so the blunt tip feels coarse as it regrows; a waxed hair has a fine, tapered tip.

blocks.note: Clients should not shave between waxes. Shaving cuts the hair at the surface, so there is nothing to grip at the next wax, and the client has to wait again until the hair is long enough (about 5 mm or the length the maker says, often about the length of a grain of rice).
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The consultation protects the client and you. Do it in private, explain the treatment, fill in the record card together and have the client sign it before you start.

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: Medical history: diabetes, poor circulation, heart or circulation problems, epilepsy, skin conditions
These can mean slow healing, loss of feeling (so a burn is not felt) or fragile skin. Some need her doctor's advice first.
Medicines and creams, especially retinoid creams or tablets, steroids, blood thinners and antibiotics
Retinoids and steroids thin the skin so wax can tear it; blood thinners increase bruising; some antibiotics make skin sensitive to heat and sun.
Allergies: rosin (colophony) in some waxes, plasters, bleach, fragrance, latex
Some people react to rosin. Choose another wax, or do a test.
Recent treatments: sunburn, sunbed, peel, laser, waxing, scar
Recently treated or sun-damaged skin is thin and tender.
How she removes hair now (shaving, cream, previous waxing)
Shaving means the hair may be too short; some creams irritate the skin.
Pregnancy
Skin can be more sensitive; follow the maker's advice and the Centre's rules.
What she wants and how often she can come
Sets her expectations and her plan.

head: Prevents waxing on that area (refer to a doctor where needed)
Restricts waxing (adapt or avoid the area)
rows: Infections: boils, impetigo, folliculitis, fungal infections, cold sores (for lip waxing), warts
Open cuts, grazes, burns, sores or rashes
Recent scars, stitches or surgery
Sunburn or windburn; recent sunbed use
Inflamed or very irritated skin; severe eczema or psoriasis flare-ups
Fever or illness
Allergy to the wax or its ingredients
Varicose veins: do not wax over them; work only on the clear skin around
Moles, warts and skin tags: do not wax over them; work around
Thin, fragile or loose skin (older clients, or those on retinoids or steroids)
Diabetes or loss of feeling: extra care; ask for her doctor's approval first
Bruising, swelling or recent injury: avoid the area
Very sensitive skin: patch test; use hot wax rather than strip wax
Pregnancy: follow the Centre's rules

blocks.note: Do not wax over moles, warts, skin tags, varicose veins, cuts, sunburn or inflamed skin. If you are unsure about any mark, do not wax it, and ask your instructor or advise her to see a doctor. A mole that changes size, colour or shape needs a doctor.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not name a disease. Explain kindly, in private, that you cannot treat the area today, advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist, record what you saw and offer to rebook.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Wax:** a small test patch on the client (for example, on the inside of the arm or on a small area to be waxed) checks her skin's reaction to the heat and the wax. Do it before every first treatment and whenever you change wax.
**Bleach:** a skin test about 24 to 48 hours before, or as the maker states (see the bleaching section).
**Depilatory cream:** a skin test as the maker states, before every use.

sections.title: Setting up and working safely and hygienically

ul: Put it on a **stable trolley** (or sturdy surface) near a socket, away from the client's legs, with the **cable tidy** so that no one can trip or pull it down.
Check the plug and cable for damage before you switch on; do not use it if either is damaged.
Switch it on early so the wax melts; set the **thermostat** as the maker says. The thermostat keeps the wax at a steady temperature.
Do not overfill, and do not heat wax in a container that is not made for it, or on a stove or in a microwave unless the maker says so.
Never leave a heater switched on and unattended, and never leave it on overnight.
Never let water or oil into the wax unless the maker allows it; keep the lid on when not in use.
Switch off at the end, let it cool, then clean it as the maker says.

head: Wax
Typical working temperature
Note
rows: Warm (strip) wax
About 40 to 45 °C (comfortably warm, like a warm bath)
Follow the maker. Hotter wax runs and burns.
Hot (hard) wax
About 45 to 55 °C, as the maker says
Thicker; sets on the skin.

blocks.p: These figures vary with the wax and the heater. The maker's temperature is the only correct one. **Wax that is hotter than the maker states can burn the client's skin.** Stir the wax before you test it, because the wax at the bottom can be hotter than the wax at the top.

flow: Stir the wax
Take a little on a clean spatula
Test it on **your inner wrist**
Apply a small amount to a small area of the **client's** skin and ask how it feels
Wait for her answer before you go on

blocks.note: Wax that feels comfortable on your wrist may still feel hot on a client with thin or sensitive skin. Always test on the client too, in an area you are about to wax, and ask her how it feels.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Cover the couch with fresh couch roll and the floor with paper or a mat, so wax drops do not reach the floor and no one slips.
Wear **disposable gloves**: waxing can raise tiny spots of blood and tissue fluid.
Tie hair back; wear an apron; keep nails short.
Keep the work area uncluttered, with the lined, lidded bin and the sharps box within reach.

head: Point
What you do
rows: Hands
Wash before and after every client; gloves on during the treatment.
Spatulas
A **new spatula for every dip** into the wax. Once a spatula has touched the skin, it never goes back in the pot: it would carry germs into the wax.
Strips, spatulas, cotton, gloves, used wax
Used once, then into the lined, lidded bin. Waste with blood on it is sealed in a bag and disposed of as the Centre's rules say.
Wax that has touched a client
Never reused.
Tweezers and scissors
Clean, then disinfect for the full contact time the maker gives, or sterilise.
Blades and lancets
Used once, then the sharps box.
Couch, trolley, heater lid
Wiped with disinfectant; fresh couch roll for every client.
Towels
Fresh for every client; used ones into a closed laundry bin.

blocks.note: Disposable gloves, couch roll and single-use spatulas protect both you and the client from germs and blood. Never use the same gloves for two clients.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Hot wax is flammable if overheated, and the heater is an electric appliance: keep it away from water, check the cable and plug, and know where the fire extinguisher is. Jamaica's power supply is 110 V at 50 Hz, so make sure the heater is made for the socket you use. A power cut can leave the wax half melted: switch the heater off at the socket and do not use it until it works normally.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Move the wax away from the skin at once.
Cool the burn immediately under **cool running water** for about 20 minutes. No ice, butter, oil or creams.
Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing; do not burst any blisters.
Get first aid or medical help for anything larger than a small area, anything that blisters, or any burn on the face or genitals.
Record it in the accident book and on the record card, and tell your supervisor.

sections.title: Preparing the client and the skin

flow: Wash your hands and put on gloves
Position the client comfortably on the couch; protect her clothing with paper or towels
Check the hair length: trim long hair with clean scissors
Clean the area with **pre-wax lotion** and dry it
Dust with a little powder only if the wax maker advises it
Check the direction of hair growth
Stir and test the wax

head: Step
Why
rows: Clean the skin with pre-wax lotion
Removes oil, sweat, creams and dead skin, so the wax grips the hair and not the skin. It also cleans the skin of germs.
Trim hair longer than about 2 cm to about 1 cm
Long hair tangles in the wax and hurts more. Hair that is too short (under about 5 mm) will not grip.
Powder (light dusting)
Dries the skin so warm wax grips the hair; some waxes do not need it.
Check the direction of growth
Wax is applied **with** the growth and removed **against** it. Hair on the legs mostly grows downward; on the underarm it often grows in several directions.
Position the client
So the skin can be held taut and the area reached without strain for either of you.

blocks.note: Never wax a client whose hair is too short, or who has shaved in the last few days: the wax cannot grip it. Explain, and ask her to come back when the hair is about 5 mm or as the maker says.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Check growth direction; test the wax on your wrist, then on the client
Hold a new spatula at about 45° and spread a thin, even layer of wax in the **direction of hair growth**
Cover an area slightly smaller than the strip
Press the strip on firmly **with** the growth, leaving a free end to hold
Hold the skin taut with your other hand
Pull the strip off quickly **against** the growth, close and parallel to the skin
Press your hand on the area at once to soothe it
Work in an order, new spatula for each dip
Remove stray hairs with clean tweezers
Remove wax residue with after-wax oil and finish with a soothing lotion

head: Point
Why
rows: Apply with the growth, remove against it
The wax coats the hair in the direction it lies; pulling against it removes the whole hair from its root, with less risk of breaking it.
Thin, even layer
Thick wax is hard to remove, hurts more and leaves residue; too thin tears and does not grip.
Pull quickly, close to the skin
A fast, low pull hurts less and does not lift the skin; pulling up and away lifts the skin and bruises it.
Hold the skin taut
Reduces pain and stops bruising and the top layer of skin lifting.
Press the hand on the area
Eases the sting and soothes the skin.
No re-waxing the same place
Going over the same area again and again can lift the top layer of skin. Use tweezers for strays.
Use a new spatula for each dip
Stops germs from the skin getting into the wax.

blocks.p: **Hot (hard) wax** is a thicker wax. It is applied in a thicker layer, with a thicker edge at the end, sets on the skin and is removed **without a strip**. It shrinks around the hair and grips it, rather than sticking to the skin, so it is gentler on delicate, thin or sensitive skin and grips short, coarse hair well.

head: Point
Warm (strip) wax
Hot (hard) wax
rows: Texture
Soft, runny; spread thinly
Thick; applied in a thicker layer
Removal
A paper or fabric strip
Flicked up by the edge once set; no strip
Best for
Large areas: legs, arms, back
Small, delicate areas: underarm, bikini line, upper lip, brows; short or coarse hair; sensitive skin
Speed
Quick over large areas
Slower: small areas
Grip on short hair
Less
Better

flow: Ask the client to rest her hand behind her head, with the skin taut
Clean the area with pre-wax lotion; dry it well; trim long hair
Look at the hair growth: it often grows in more than one direction; plan small sections
Test the wax on your wrist, then on a small area of her skin
Spread wax in the direction of growth, leaving a thicker edge to grip
When it has set but is still bendy, hold the skin taut, flick up the edge and remove it quickly against the growth, close to the skin
Do the next section; repeat for the other direction of growth
Press the area to soothe; remove stray hairs with tweezers; soothing lotion

blocks.note: Hot wax that has set too hard cracks and breaks; wax that has not set rips the skin. Practise judging 'set but still bendy' on a small area. The wax should lift cleanly with the hair inside it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Sugaring** uses a paste made mostly of **sugar**, with water and lemon (or another acid) cooked together. It is applied by hand or spatula **against** the direction of growth, and flicked off **with** the growth. Because the paste follows the hair, it is usually gentle, and it can be washed off with water. It removes hair from the root. Sugaring paste is a sugar-based paste, not a chemical cream.

head: Treatment area
Method and points
rows: Legs and arms
Warm strip wax in large sections is quickest; sugaring or hot wax is gentler.
Underarm
Hot wax or sugaring; small sections, because the hair grows in several directions; hold the skin taut.
Upper lip and chin
Hot wax or sugaring; small areas; check for cold sores first; no wax near the nostrils.
Brows
Hot wax or tweezers; keep wax away from the eye (see the lash and brow unit).
Bikini line and intimate areas
Specialist skills, privacy and extra consent; follow the Centre's rules.

ul: A **depilatory cream** is a chemical cream that dissolves the hair at the skin's surface. It does not remove the root, so hair returns in a few days.
The main risk is that it can **burn or irritate the skin**. Do a skin test as the maker states, before every use, and follow the timing exactly.
Never use it on broken, sunburnt or irritated skin, on the face unless made for it, or near the eyes.
Remove wax left on the skin with **after-wax oil** or lotion on cotton, wiping with the growth.
Check for stray hairs; remove them with clean tweezers.
Apply a **soothing lotion** or gel.
Do not use perfumed products straight after: they sting and can cause allergic reactions on open follicles.

blocks.p: **Hair bleach** lightens dark hair on the face and body (upper lip, forearms, legs) so it is less noticeable. It does not remove the hair, so no regrowth problems, but the hair stays; as new hair grows, the dark roots show and the client needs another treatment after a few weeks.

ul: Most hair bleach for the face and body is made of **hydrogen peroxide cream** mixed with an **activator** (powder) just before use.
Use only bleach made for face and body hair, as the maker says. **Never** use household bleach, hair-colour bleach made for the head, or a product that claims to lighten skin.
Do not mix brands, and mix only what you need: leftover bleach cannot be kept.

Do a **skin test** about 24 to 48 hours before, or as the maker states, on a small area (behind the ear, or the inner forearm). Read it before you mix: redness, itching, swelling or burning means a positive result, so do not bleach.
Check for contraindications: broken, sore, sunburnt or irritated skin; cuts; recent waxing, peels or laser on the area; skin infections; known allergy to bleach. No bleach near the eyes.
Explain that bleach lightens the hair, does not remove it, and does not lighten the skin; on very dark skin, bleached hair can look golden and stand out. Agree on what she wants.
Do not bleach and wax the same area on the same day: wax first, if she wants both, and wait a few days; bleach on freshly waxed skin burns.

flow: Protect the client's clothing; wash your hands; put on gloves
Clean the area so it is free of grease; dry it well
Work in a well-ventilated room
Mix the cream and activator in a **non-metallic** bowl, exactly as the maker says
Apply an even layer over the hair with a spatula, in the direction of growth, keeping it off broken skin and well away from the eyes
Start the timer; stay with the client
Check every few minutes: how light is the hair? any redness, stinging or itching?
If the skin reacts, remove the bleach at once
When the hair is light enough, remove the bleach with damp cotton and rinse with **cool** water
Apply a soothing lotion; record the treatment

ul: Check by wiping a little off a test strip of hair with damp cotton. Never leave the bleach on longer than the maker's time.
Cool water soothes the skin; hot water irritates it.
Throw away leftover bleach; empty containers and used cotton go in a lined, lidded bin.
Keep bleach in its labelled container, lid tight, in a cool, dry, dark place away from heat, out of reach of children.

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Bleach in the eye
Rinse at once with plenty of clean, cool water or eye wash, and get medical help.
Skin burns, stings or reddens
Remove the bleach at once; rinse with plenty of cool water; apply soothing lotion; record it; advise a doctor if it does not settle.
Hair not light enough
Do not go over it again the same day; check the mix, the time and the skin test. Book a repeat after the skin settles.
Orange or yellow tone on dark hair
Normal: dark hair lightens through red and gold. Explain this at the consultation.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican clients have deep skin tones and dark hair. Bleached hair on very dark skin can look golden or orange and stand out more than the original dark hair. Explain this before you start, and offer to bleach a small test area.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Contra-action
What you see
What you do
rows: Redness and small raised bumps
Pink skin and bumps around the follicles straight after treatment.
Normal: a short-term reaction to the hair being removed; usually settles within a few hours. Soothing lotion; a cool compress.
Blood spots
Tiny spots at the follicles, especially with strong hair on the legs.
Gloves on; wipe with antiseptic on clean cotton; dispose of it in a lined, sealed bag or bin.
A burn
Red, painful skin, blisters.
Cool under cool running water about 20 minutes; no creams or butter; first aid; record.
Skin lifting or tearing
A raw patch where the top layer came away.
Stop; apply a soothing antiseptic; advise her to keep it clean and out of sun; do not wax it again; record.
Bruising
Dark marks where the skin was not held taut or the pull was too hard.
Prevent by holding the skin taut and pulling low.
Allergic reaction
A rash, itching, swelling.
Stop; remove the product; cool compress; advise a doctor.
Ingrown hairs
Hairs growing under the skin, a few days later; red bumps.
Advise gentle exfoliation after a few days; no picking.
Folliculitis
Red, pus-filled spots at the follicles.
Do not wax until healed; advise a doctor or pharmacist.

blocks.p: **Folliculitis** is an infection of the hair follicles that shows as red, pus-filled spots. It happens after waxing or shaving, usually because of germs entering the open follicles.

Some waxes contain **rosin** (colophony), a natural resin that helps wax grip. Some people are allergic to it, so ask about allergies at the consultation and offer a rosin-free wax if she is allergic.

head: Advice
Why
rows: For about 24 to 48 hours, avoid hot baths, saunas, sunbathing, sunbeds, and sea or pool swimming
The follicles are open and the skin is sensitive; heat, sun, salt and chlorine irritate it.
Avoid perfumed lotions, deodorant (after an underarm wax for about a day) and tight clothing
Perfume and friction irritate the skin and cause spots.
Do not touch, scratch or pick the area
Germs on the fingers can get into the open follicles.
After a few days, exfoliate gently, then regularly; moisturise
Helps prevent ingrown hairs.
Do not shave between waxes
Shaving cuts the hair short and spoils the next wax.
Wear a sunscreen on the waxed skin when it is exposed to the sun
Freshly waxed skin burns more easily; sun can also darken the skin.
Book the next wax in about 4 to 6 weeks; call the salon if there is lasting redness, spots or soreness
Hair is long enough to wax again; problems are caught early.

blocks.p: After bleaching, advise her to keep the skin out of strong sun for a day, use a soothing lotion, and tell you at once if she has stinging or redness. Another bleach is usually needed in about 4 weeks as the hair grows.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's details, signature
07/11/2026, Shaunette Burke, Mandeville; signed
Medical details, medicines and allergies
No medicines; no allergies; no varicose veins seen
Skin tests
Bleach test 05/11/2026 behind ear, negative
Area, wax and product
Lower legs; warm wax with a rosin-free formula; thermostat set as the maker says
Reactions
Mild redness, settled before she left
Advice given
Aftercare sheet; no shaving; exfoliate after 3 days; rebook in 5 weeks
Therapist
Trainee's name, checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Record cards are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure; waxing involves private areas of the body, so be especially careful never to discuss a client's treatment with others.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Switch off the heater and let it cool
Bin spatulas, strips, gloves, cotton and used wax in the lined, lidded bin; seal blood-stained waste
Clean and disinfect tweezers and scissors; blades to the sharps box
Wipe the heater (as the maker says), trolley and couch with disinfectant
Fresh couch roll; used towels into the laundry bin
Wash your hands

ul: I can explain epilation, depilation and bleaching, and the types of hair.
I can describe anagen, catagen and telogen and say why hair does not all grow back at once.
I can carry out a consultation and say why I ask about medicines, diabetes, allergies and recent treatments.
I can name the contraindications that prevent waxing and those that restrict it.
I can set up a wax heater safely, test the temperature on my wrist and then on the client, and say why.
I can keep waxing hygienic: gloves, new spatula every dip, lined bin, sharps box.
I can prepare the skin with pre-wax lotion and trim long hair.
I can give a half-leg warm wax, applying with the growth and removing against it, skin held taut.
I can compare warm and hot wax and use hot wax on the underarm.
I can explain sugaring and depilatory creams and their risks.
I can carry out a skin test, mix and apply bleach safely, check it often and rinse with cool water.
I can give first aid for a burn and for bleach in the eye.
I can recognise redness, blood spots, lifted skin, folliculitis and ingrown hairs and say what to do.
I can give aftercare and home-care advice and complete the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I test the wax on my inner wrist, then on a small area of the client's skin, so that I do not burn her.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Removing hair at the surface of the skin.
Lightening hair so it shows less; it does not remove it.
The small pocket in the skin from which a hair grows.
The part at the base of the follicle that feeds the hair with blood.
The growing stage of the hair cycle.
The short changing stage when the hair stops growing and leaves its blood supply.
The resting stage before the hair falls out.
Fine, soft, short hair covering most of the body.
Thick, coarse, darker hair, such as under the arms and on the legs.
Something that prevents a treatment or means it must be changed.
An unwanted reaction during or after a treatment.
Swollen, twisted veins, often on the legs; never waxed over.
A skin medicine (cream or tablet) that thins the skin.
A natural resin in some waxes; some people are allergic to it.
The part of the heater that keeps the wax at a steady temperature.
A cleansing lotion that removes oil, sweat and creams before waxing.
A soft wax removed with a strip.
A thicker wax that sets and is removed without a strip.
The flat tool used to spread wax.
The paper or fabric piece pressed onto warm wax and pulled off.
Removing hair from the root with a sugar-based paste.
A chemical cream that dissolves hair at the surface.
Oil that removes small bits of wax left on the skin.
Putting a used spatula back in the wax pot, which carries germs into it.
The chemical in bleach cream that lightens hair.
The powder mixed with bleach cream to start the lightening.
A small test on the skin, 24 to 48 hours before, to check for a reaction.
A hair that curls back and grows under the skin.
An infection of the hair follicles, with red, pus-filled spots.
A rigid container for used blades.
The client's record of checks, tests, treatments, reactions and advice.

c1.title: A first leg wax in Portmore
c1.text: Nadine Francis, 24, has her first leg wax at a salon in Portmore. She has shaved her legs three days ago, so the hair is only a few millimetres long. Trainee Tanisha turns on the wax heater, cuts the plastic tie on the cable to move it, and balances the heater on a stool beside the couch. When the wax looks runny, she tests it on a cotton pad and starts at once, applying it against the direction of growth.

c2.title: A client with a medical history in Spanish Town
c2.text: Mrs. Beverly Hanson, 58, wants her lower legs waxed at the Centre's salon in Spanish Town. She has type 2 diabetes, takes tablets for it, and says she sometimes cannot feel her feet properly. There are large, knotted varicose veins on the back of her right calf, and a small raised mole on her left shin with a few dark hairs growing from it.

c3.title: Underarm hot wax in Ocho Rios
c3.text: Shantelle Williams, 30, a hotel receptionist in Ocho Rios, wants her underarms waxed. Trainee Marlon notes that the hair grows in different directions and is short and coarse. He tests the wax on his wrist, finds it fine, and applies it. When he lifts the edge of a patch, it comes away with a small area of raw, shiny skin, and Shantelle winces. He then dips the same spatula back into the pot for the next patch.

c4.title: A bleach for a bride in Black River
c4.text: Kerry-Ann Powell, 27, a bride in Black River, wants the dark hair on her forearms bleached before her wedding on Saturday. It is Thursday morning. She has very deep skin and has not had a skin test. Trainee Orlando mixes the cream and activator in a metal bowl, and the room's windows are shut because it is raining. Ten minutes after he starts, Kerry-Ann says her arm is stinging.

c5.title: Aftercare and a rash in Mandeville
c5.text: Gillian Ferguson, 35, had her legs waxed in a Mandeville salon yesterday. Today she goes to the beach, applies a perfumed body lotion, shaves a few stray hairs and wears tight jeans. That night she sees small red spots, some with pus, around the follicles on her shins, and calls the salon.

questions.q: What should Tanisha have done about the length of Nadine's hair?
o: Waxed it anyway, using a thicker layer of wax
Asked her to come back when the hair is long enough
Trimmed the hairs even shorter with the scissors
Applied the wax twice to catch the short hairs
questions.why: Hair shorter than about 5 mm (or the maker's length) cannot be gripped, so waxing it would hurt and leave the hairs behind. Explain, and ask the client to come back when the hair is long enough. She must not shave between waxes.

questions.q: What is wrong with the way the heater has been set up?
o: Nothing, as long as the stool is steady enough
The cable is too long and should be wound around the heater
It is on a stool beside the couch, with the cable tie cut
It should sit on the floor so it cannot fall off a trolley
questions.why: A wax heater belongs on a stable trolley with the cable tidy and clear of walkways, and the client's legs. A heater beside the couch on a stool can be knocked over, and cutting the cable tie leaves a tripping hazard.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to test the wax on a cotton pad only?
o: Cotton pads soak up wax and always show it as too cool
Cotton pads will make the wax cool down too quickly
A pad shows the colour, not the thickness of the wax
A pad cannot show how the heat feels on skin
questions.why: Wax is tested on your inner wrist and then on a small area of the client's own skin, with her telling you how it feels. Only skin shows how the heat will feel to her.

questions.q: Tanisha applied the wax against the direction of growth. What is the correct way?
o: Apply against the growth, then pull the strip with the growth
Apply with the growth, and pull the strip off against it
Apply in circles, then pull the strip straight up
Apply with the growth, and pull the strip off with it
questions.why: Wax coats the hairs in the direction they lie, and a quick pull back against the growth, close to the skin, takes the whole hair out from the root. Pulling straight up lifts the skin and bruises it.

questions.q: How should the therapist handle Mrs. Hanson's diabetes and reduced feeling?
o: Wax as normal, since diabetes does not affect the skin
Use hotter wax, because she cannot feel the heat anyway
Refuse all treatments, whatever her doctor says
Take extra care and ask for her doctor's approval
questions.why: Diabetes can slow healing and reduce feeling, so a burn may go unnoticed. The safest course is extra care and her doctor's approval before any waxing; wax must never be hotter than the maker states.

questions.q: What should be done about the varicose veins on her right calf?
o: Wax over them firmly, to help the veins shrink
Wax them first, before the rest of the leg
Do not wax them; work only on clear skin
Use hot wax on them and warm wax elsewhere
questions.why: Varicose veins are fragile and can bleed or bruise badly if waxed. They are a restriction: leave them alone and wax only the unaffected skin.

questions.q: What should be done about the mole on her left shin?
o: Cover it with wax and remove it with the hairs
Wax round it and leave the mole alone
Trim the mole flat with scissors before waxing
Wax it last, once the other hairs are removed
questions.why: Wax can pull and tear a mole, causing bleeding. Work around it. If it has changed in size, colour or shape, advise her to see a doctor.

questions.q: What probably caused the raw, shiny skin on Shantelle's underarm?
o: Wax that was set too hard, or skin that was not held taut
Wax that was applied in the direction of the hair growth
A test of the wax on the therapist's wrist
Applying wax in small sections instead of one large patch
questions.why: Skin lifts when it is not held taut, when wax is pulled upward, or when the skin is thin or the area has been waxed repeatedly. Apply with the growth and remove quickly against it, with the skin held firm.

questions.q: What is wrong with dipping the same spatula back in the pot?
o: The spatula will snap off in the wax pot
It carries germs into the wax
It makes the wax too cool to work with
It changes the colour of the wax
questions.why: A spatula that has touched the skin carries germs and tissue fluid, which then contaminate the wax and are passed to the next client. Use a new spatula for every dip.

questions.q: What should Marlon do about the raw patch?
o: Stop; apply soothing antiseptic, no more wax there
Wax over it again to remove the hairs left behind
Rub it hard with a dry towel to clear any wax
Cover it with perfumed powder to dry it out
questions.why: Lifted skin is a contra-action: stop, apply a soothing antiseptic, keep the area clean and out of the sun, record it, and do not wax that area again until healed.

questions.q: Why should hot wax be applied with a thicker edge at the end of each patch?
o: So that the edge can be gripped once the wax has set
So that the wax cools faster and stays on the skin longer
So that a paper strip can be pressed onto it afterwards
So that the hairs under the thicker edge are removed twice
questions.why: Hot wax is removed without a strip, so you need an edge thick enough to flick up and hold once the wax has set but is still bendy. Nothing is pressed on top of it.

questions.q: What should Orlando have done before today's treatment?
o: A skin test about 24 to 48 hours before
A strong exfoliation, so the bleach can soak in
Waxed the forearms the same morning for best results
Applied heavy oil so the bleach would slide on
questions.why: A skin test about 24 to 48 hours before, or as the maker states, shows an allergy before it reaches a big area. Bleach on freshly waxed or exfoliated skin burns, and oily skin stops it spreading evenly.

questions.q: What should Orlando do now that Kerry-Ann's arm is stinging?
o: Leave it on, as stinging means the bleach is working
Remove the bleach at once and rinse with cool water
Add more bleach so it works faster and finishes soon
Rinse it with hot water to wash it off quickly
questions.why: Stinging, redness or itching means the skin is reacting. Remove the bleach immediately with damp cotton, rinse with plenty of cool water, apply a soothing lotion, record it and advise a doctor if it does not settle.

questions.q: Which of Orlando's set-up mistakes is a safety risk from fumes?
o: The bowl is too small for the bleach
The cream is mixed with a plastic spatula
The activator is added after the cream
The room has no air flow, with windows shut
questions.why: Bleach fumes can irritate the eyes and nose, so mix and apply in a well-ventilated room. The bowl is also wrong: it must be non-metallic, because metal can react with the peroxide.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann's wedding is on Saturday. What is the best advice?
o: Bleach today anyway, as the day before is too late
Skip the skin test since the wedding is soon
Do the skin test now, then bleach on Saturday
Wax the forearms on Friday, then bleach on Saturday
questions.why: Do the skin test now and read it before bleaching. Bleach on freshly waxed skin burns. If the test is negative she can be bleached on the day, or earlier; if it is positive she must not be bleached.

questions.q: Which of Gillian's actions most likely caused the red, pus-filled spots?
o: Waxing against the direction of growth
Perfume, shaving, tight jeans and the beach
A skin test done 24 hours before the wax
Using a mild soothing lotion after the wax
questions.why: After waxing, the follicles stay open for 24 to 48 hours, so heat, salt, perfume, shaving and friction irritate them and let germs in, which can lead to folliculitis.

questions.q: What should the salon advise Gillian to do about the spots?
o: Squeeze each one to clear the pus, then wax again
Cover the spots with perfumed powder and keep swimming
Leave them alone, keep clean, and see a doctor
Shave the area to remove the hairs that are infected
questions.why: Pus-filled spots at the follicles suggest an infection. She should not squeeze, shave or wax the area; keep it clean, avoid heat and perfume, and see a doctor or pharmacist. The salon records it.

questions.q: A client says she shaves 'to make the hair grow back finer'. What is the correct fact?
o: Shaving and waxing both stop the hair from regrowing
Shaving cuts at the surface and does not change growth
Waxing changes the hair into a coarser kind of hair
Shaving removes the root, so the hair is finer
questions.why: Neither shaving nor waxing changes the hair's thickness or colour. Shaving cuts at the surface (the blunt tip feels coarse), and hair soon returns; waxing removes it from the root.

questions.q: A client asks which hair has just come away from its blood supply and is about to rest. Which stage is this?
o: Telogen
Anagen
Vellus
Catagen
questions.why: Catagen is the short changing stage, when the hair stops growing and comes away from its blood supply. Anagen is growing, and telogen is resting.

questions.q: A client is on a retinoid cream. Why must you take care before waxing her?
o: The cream makes the wax set too hard to remove
The cream makes the hair grow back on the same day
The cream makes the wax melt at a lower temperature
The cream thins the skin, so the wax can tear it
questions.why: Retinoids thin the skin, so waxing can lift or tear it. Ask about creams and tablets at every consultation, and avoid waxing the treated area or follow her doctor's advice.
